summary: Explains what Mobile IP is meant for, summarizes its key features, and shows that it satisfied the requirements for advancing to Proposed Standard. It is an applicability statement accompanying the main Mobile IP specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains what Mobile IP is designed to do and summarizes the working group's evidence for advancing its specification. It also describes the protocol's limits and its security requirements.

subtitle: An applicability statement for Mobile IP and evidence for its advancement to Proposed Standard.

tldr.problem: The Mobile IP working group needed to describe where the protocol applies and show that it met the requirements to advance.
tldr.mechanism: The statement summarizes Mobile IP routing, scope, security, and a reported interoperability test.
tldr.outcome: The co-chairs concluded that the criteria for Proposed Standard had been met.

facts.label: Minimum required authentication
facts.value: Keyed MD5 with manual key distribution

today: RFC 2005 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How Mobile IP Routes Packets
sections.content:
Mobile IP lets a node change its Internet attachment point without changing its IP address, so transport and higher-layer connections can continue. Packets for the node first reach its home network, where the home agent tunnels them to the node's most recently reported care-of address.

At the tunnel endpoint, the inner packet is removed and delivered to the mobile node. Packets sent by the mobile node use standard IP routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The node keeps its home address while away. A home agent forwards incoming packets through a tunnel to the node's current care-of address.

sections.title: Where Mobile IP Applies
sections.content:
The statement describes Mobile IP as suitable for movement between IP subnets, across similar or different media. It calls this the macro mobility problem and says link-layer handoff may suit movement among small-area wireless transceivers better.

Without route optimization, a home agent can become a load point for many mobile nodes. The statement says more home agents can be added or dynamically discovered. Mobile IP does not address IP address renumbering.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IP is for movement between subnets. The RFC says it is less suited to very small local handoffs and does not solve address renumbering.

sections.title: Security and Advancement Evidence
sections.content:
Registration messages between a mobile node and its home agent require cryptographically strong authentication and replay protection using timestamps or nonces. Implementations must support keyed MD5 with manual key distribution. Agent discovery messages are not required to be authenticated.

The RFC reports interoperability testing at an interim meeting held October 23-27, 1995. At least two independent implementations interoperated on all listed features. The co-chairs concluded that the RFC 1264 requirements for advancement to Proposed Standard were satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: Registration must be authenticated, while discovery messages need not be. The RFC reports that independent implementations worked together in the tests it describes.
